lines: Splitting a keyspace, agreeing on a write inside one piece of it, and coordinating several pieces together.
Every one of those three pieces was already built, on its own, earlier in this chapter.
Watch one real database run all three of them together, on every single write it handles.
Commit to an answer before the reveal.
This pattern a real distributed database actually runs on. Does it need some genuinely new mechanism nobody's built yet?
Or is the whole thing made entirely out of pieces this chapter already covered?
answer: It's tempting to assume reaching global scale needs an entirely new trick.

But a write touching two separate pieces of the keyspace really does just chain what's already there: each piece agrees on its own slice first, and a separate coordinating step gets both slices to agree together.
So no new mechanism. Just the pieces already built, chained together correctly.

lines: Watch that exact chain, measured directly, on a transaction touching two separate pieces of the keyspace.
Each piece reaches its own internal agreement completely on its own, independently of the other.
Only once both have done that does a coordinating step get the two of them to agree with each other.
Now feed one real, troubling input into a clock that has to assign these timestamps.
Give its physical readings a genuine skew, twice, where the clock briefly jumps backward instead of forward.
Watch its actual output anyway. Every single timestamp it hands out still strictly increases.
One more piece has to fit before any of this is trustworthy.
A commit gets assigned a timestamp, but has to sit and wait out its own clock's uncertainty window before anyone else is allowed to see it.
Watch what that wait actually buys: anything that starts after it is guaranteed a strictly later timestamp, no exceptions.
One more prediction before this topic's second reveal.
Two transactions are reading and changing the exact same row, and neither one ever takes a lock.
At what point does a scheme like that actually notice the two of them are in conflict?
answer: It's tempting to assume the second transaction gets stopped the instant it touches that row.
But with no lock at all standing in the way, nothing stops either one from doing its own full share of work against that row.
So the conflict only surfaces once a transaction actually tries to commit, against whatever already landed first.

lines: Here's that exact scenario, measured directly, end to end.
Both transactions read the identical row while it sits completely unlocked, the entire time.
Whichever one commits first simply succeeds. The other one only learns it lost the moment its own commit gets rejected.
One real cost sits underneath everything shown here so far.
A single machine running an ordinary database pays no extra trip across the network beyond the one its own client already made.
Spread that identical write across several pieces of a distributed keyspace, and it pays for several more trips on top.
Pull the whole topic together.

This pattern is a real composition: pieces agreeing internally, a clock that never slips backward, a wait that makes real-world ordering trustworthy, and a scheme that checks for conflicts only once work is already done.
None of it arrives for free. Every single piece of it has a real, measurable price attached.
One last one. A team's entire dataset comfortably fits on a single ordinary machine, and every one of their writes stays inside one table.
They're deciding between a fully distributed database and just running plain, ordinary Postgres on one box.
Given everything just measured here: is paying for all this distributed machinery actually worth it for them?
answer: It's tempting to assume more distributed machinery is simply the stronger, safer choice by default.
But every single cost measured in this topic exists to solve one specific problem: coordinating data that's genuinely spread across separate machines. Their data was never spread across anything.
So no. None of that machinery buys them a single thing they actually need.
